sentences.english_text: The wind looked down from high above, and what he saw made him very sad.
All the beautiful trees were burning, and animals were dying.
The wind saw the two hunters who had started the fire, and he was so angry with them that he zoomed down and blew them off a steep cliff.
And he went looking for Drippy.
The wind found him next to a burning bush, and when the wind saw Drippy, he thought, I'm afraid I'm too late.
Because the fire had started to melt Drippy, and there was only a little spot of water left.
The wind gently picked Drippy up into his arms, and Drippy was so weak that he could not even open his eyes.
The wind carried Drippy far away from the forest fire into the cool sky, and Drippy began to feel better.
The wind carried Drippy through a cloud, and some of the moisture clung to Drippy, and he could feel himself begin to grow again, until he was once more a full-size raindrop.
He opened his eyes and looked around.
He could see the fire in the far distance.
What a story we'd have to tell his cousins when he got back home.
Of course, he would not tell it exactly the way it happened.
He would have to be the hero of a story.
He would say that he had tried to put out the fire and almost got killed.
But had that stopped him?
Not at all.
Instead of running away, he stayed there to try to help to rescue some of the animals and to save the trees.
Everyone had left the forest, fleeing in panic, but brave Drippy had stayed there until the very end, making sure that everyone else was safe.
His imagination was so real to Drippy that he began to believe it himself.
When the wind saw that Drippy was better, he was very pleased.
Once again, he had saved the little raindrop.
Now he will say, thank you for saving me, thought the wind.
But all Drippy said was, that was certainly a big forest fire.
The wind was very angry with Drippy.
The wind was very angry with Drippy.
I should take him home now, but he's not ready yet.
He would just run away again.
First, he must learn his lesson.
They were over a large city, and the wind said, I'm going to put you down now, and this time I want you to wait for me.
Do you understand?
Oh, yes, Mr. Wind.
I don't want to have to go looking for you again.
Oh, no, Mr. Wind.
Very well, then.
The wind zoomed down with Drippy on his coattails, and he deposited Drippy in a park filled with statues and people and pigeons.
He put Drippy on a park bench.
I'll see you in a little while.
And he raced back up into the sky.
